## Legal research memo

**September 28, 2026.** New York Civil Rights Law §§ [50](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVR/50)–[51](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVR/51) require a parent’s or guardian’s written consent to use a minor’s name or likeness for advertising or trade; § 51 permits an injunction and damages. The missing releases do **not**, by themselves, make the box scores or highlights unlawful. The Court of Appeals protects reporting on matters of public interest, including a performance at a sporting event. Accurate clips and names tied to game coverage likely qualify, even if the app earns revenue. A player’s image used to promote the app or a sponsor presents a different risk, especially if the promotion is an advertisement in disguise. *[Gautier](https://law.justia.com/cases/new-york/court-of-appeals/1952/304-n-y-354-107-n-e-2d-485.html); [Finger](https://law.justia.com/cases/new-york/court-of-appeals/1990/77-n-y-2d-138-2.html); [Messenger](https://law.justia.com/cases/new-york/court-of-appeals/2000/94-n-y-2d-436-0.html).*

New York’s Child Data Protection Act separately restricts processing personal data **of covered app users** aged 13–17 unless it is strictly necessary for a specified purpose or the user gives informed consent. Whether a depicted player is an app user matters; appearing in a clip alone does not establish coverage. N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law §§ [899-ee](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GBS/899-EE), [899-ff](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GBS/899-FF).

Federal COPPA’s child definition is **under 13**, so being a 14-year-old subject of coverage does not trigger its parental-consent rule; younger app users may. [15 U.S.C. §§ 6501–6502](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?edition=prelim&path=%2Fprelim%40title15%2Fchapter91). FERPA and New York Education Law § 2-d matter if a school supplies protected student records or the app is its contractor. FERPA permits properly designated directory information only after notice and an opportunity to opt out. [20 U.S.C. § 1232g](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?edition=prelim&req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title20-chapter31-subchapter3-part4&saved=%7CZ3JhbnVsZWlkOlVTQy1wcmVsaW0tdGl0bGUyMC1zZWN0aW9uMTIzMmc%3D%7C%7C%7C0%7Cfalse%7Cprelim); [N.Y. Educ. Law § 2-d](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/EDN/2-D). Finally, box-score facts are uncopyrightable, but recorded footage may be protected; rights to third-party clips must be checked. [17 U.S.C. §§ 102](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=%28title%3A17+section%3A102+edition%3Aprelim%29), [106](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=%28title%3A17+section%3A106+edition%3Aprelim%29); *[NBA v. Motorola](https://openjurist.org/105/f3d/841)*.

### Legal research memo

**Conclusion.** Assuming the app independently records public games, New York law generally permits it to publish accurate box scores and game highlights naming 14-year-old players without parental releases. New York recognizes no general common-law privacy claim. Its [Civil Rights Law §§ 50–51](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVR/50) require a parent’s or guardian’s written consent when a minor’s name or likeness is used for **advertising or trade**, and allow an injunction and damages for unauthorized use. *Messenger* holds that reporting matters of public interest is ordinarily outside those provisions when the image relates to the report. Genuine game coverage likely qualifies, including in a paid app. A player’s image used to solicit subscriptions or endorse a sponsor presents a different risk under *Beverley*. [§ 51](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVR/51). [*Messenger v. Gruner + Jahr Printing & Publishing*, 94 N.Y.2d 436 (2000)](https://law.justia.com/cases/new-york/court-of-appeals/2000/94-n-y-2d-436-0.html); [*Beverley v. Choices Women’s Medical Center*, 78 N.Y.2d 745 (1991)](https://law.justia.com/cases/new-york/court-of-appeals/1991/78-n-y-2d-745-0.html).

New York’s Child Data Protection Act separately regulates personal data **collected through app use** from a covered New York user. If a known 14-year-old player uses the app, processing that user’s data generally must be necessary to provide the requested service or supported by the teen’s informed consent. Merely appearing in footage does not establish that the player is a covered *user*. [N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law §§ 899-ee](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GBS/899-EE), [899-ff](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GBS/899-FF).

Federal COPPA concerns online data collection from children **under 13**, so the players’ age alone does not trigger it. FERPA governs a covered school’s disclosure of maintained education records, not footage the app independently records. If the app receives school records, it should confirm parental consent or a properly noticed directory-information designation without an opt-out. [15 U.S.C. §§ 6501(1), 6502](https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/rules/childrens-online-privacy-protection-rule-coppa); [20 U.S.C. § 1232g](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/20/1232g); [34 C.F.R. §§ 99.3, 99.37](https://studentprivacy.ed.gov/ferpa?exp=8).

**Legal research memo (New York; September 28, 2026)**

**Signup.** Before asking for the card or consent, show the trial and renewal terms clearly beside the signup control: two months free, the date the first $49 charge will occur, annual renewal at $49, the deadline to avoid each charge, and how to cancel. Obtain affirmative, informed consent to the recurring plan before charging, then promptly send a confirmation the customer can keep containing the price, billing frequency, deadline, and cancellation instructions. Collecting a card alone does not establish that consent. [N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law §§ 527, 527-a(1)(a)–(c)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GBS/527-A); [15 U.S.C. § 8403](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?edition=prelim&num=0&req=%28title%3A15+section%3A8403+edition%3Aprelim%29).

**Reminders.** Because the trial exceeds one month, send a reminder with cancellation instructions **3–21 days before the deadline for the first charge**, through the customer’s selected notification channel. The separate free-trial statute may require the trial terms and deadline **15–30 days before that deadline**; its exception for certain subscriptions depends on the actual commitment and purchase terms. Sending one complete reminder **15–21 days before the deadline** satisfies both timing rules if that statute applies. For each later annual renewal, send a cancellation reminder **15–45 days before its cancellation deadline**. [N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law §§ 527-a(1)(f), (h)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GBS/527-A), [396-mm(1)–(2)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GBS/396-MM).

**Cancellation.** Let customers cancel at any time through a simple mechanism as easy as signup, in the same medium they used; offer cancellation through every medium in which the business accepts consent. An online signup therefore needs online cancellation. A retention offer cannot obstruct or delay the request. Federal law likewise requires a simple way to stop recurring charges; the First Department held that scripted, multi-stage cancellation with repeated retention pressure violated that requirement. [N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law § 527-a(1)(d)–(e)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GBS/527-A); [15 U.S.C. § 8403](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?edition=prelim&num=0&req=%28title%3A15+section%3A8403+edition%3Aprelim%29); [*Matter of People v Sirius XM Radio Inc.*, 243 A.D.3d 424 (1st Dep’t 2025)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2025/2025_06145.htm).

**Legal research memo — New York, September 28, 2026**

The app is an automatic renewal offer to New York consumers. Before asking for a card **or** consent, the signup screen must conspicuously display, near the consent request, the app being sold, the two month trial, when the first $49 charge occurs, the $49 yearly renewal, the cancellation deadline, and how to cancel. The startup must obtain affirmative consent to those terms before charging the card; supplying a card alone is insufficient. It must promptly send a confirmation the customer can keep, repeating the price, charge frequency, deadline, and cancellation methods. [N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law §§ 527, 527-a(1)(a)–(c)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GBS/527-A); [15 U.S.C. § 8403](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?edition=prelim&num=0&req=%28title%3A15+section%3A8403+edition%3Aprelim%29).

Because the trial exceeds one month, the startup must send a reminder **3–21 days before the deadline to avoid the first charge**. Because the paid term is one year and renews for another year, it must also send a reminder **15–45 days before each renewal’s cancellation deadline**. Each reminder must explain how to cancel and use the notification channel the customer selected. [N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law § 527-a(1)(f), (h)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GBS/527-A).

Customers must be able to cancel at any time through a simple mechanism as easy as signup, in the same medium and every medium the startup accepts for consent. An online or in-app signup therefore needs online or in-app cancellation; a required phone call, obstructive steps, or delayed processing would violate the statute. Federal law likewise requires a simple way to stop recurring charges. The New York Appellate Division held that a multistage script, repeated retention offers, and pressure tactics were not “simple” under federal law. [N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law § 527-a(1)(d)–(e)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GBS/527-A); [15 U.S.C. § 8403(3)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?edition=prelim&num=0&req=%28title%3A15+section%3A8403+edition%3Aprelim%29); [*Matter of People v. Sirius XM Radio Inc.*, 243 A.D.3d 424 (1st Dep’t 2025)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2025/2025_06145.htm).

**Conclusion: No.** Assuming the website is operated by nonlawyers, taking 15% of the fees law firms collect from referred homeowners would share legal fees with a nonlawyer, contrary to [Rule 5.4(a)](https://www.nycourts.gov/ad3/agc/rules/22NYCRR-Part-1200.pdf). [Rule 7.2(a)](https://www.nycourts.gov/ad3/agc/rules/22NYCRR-Part-1200.pdf) also bars lawyers from paying a person or organization to obtain client employment or reward a resulting recommendation. Calling the payment a marketing fee would not change its link to the referred clients’ legal fees.

[Judiciary Law § 491(1)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/JUD/491) separately prohibits a nonlawyer from receiving part of an attorney’s fee in consideration for placing a claim or demand with the attorney; subdivision (2) makes a violation a misdemeanor. New York appellate courts have held nonlawyer fee sharing agreements illegal and unenforceable. *[Bonilla v. Rotter](https://www.nycourts.gov/REPORTER/3dseries/2007/2007_00449.htm)*, 36 A.D.3d 534, 535 (1st Dep’t 2007); *[Ballan v. Sirota](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2018/2018_05014.htm)*, 163 A.D.3d 516, 517 (2d Dep’t 2018).

The website may explore ordinary advertising or lead generation instead, but any payment must comply with Rule 5.4 and the conditions in [Rule 7.2 comment 1](https://www.nycourts.gov/ad3/agc/rules/22NYCRR-Part-1200.pdf), including that the service not recommend the lawyers. A 15% share of collected legal fees does not qualify.

**Legal research memo**

**Question.** May a website receive 15% of the fees New York law firms collect from homeowners it refers for property tax assessment challenges?

**Answer.** Assuming the website is a commercial, nonlawyer business, no. New York prohibits a lawyer from sharing legal fees with a nonlawyer. A payment calculated as 15% of each referred client’s legal fee is fee sharing, whatever the parties call it. [22 N.Y.C.R.R. § 1200.0, Rule 5.4(a)](https://www.nycourts.gov/ad3/agc/rules/22NYCRR-Part-1200.pdf). Judiciary Law § 491 also prohibits a person or company from receiving part of an attorney’s fee as consideration for placing a civil claim or demand with that attorney; violation is a misdemeanor. [N.Y. Jud. Law § 491](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/JUD/491).

New York appellate courts refuse to enforce nonlawyer fee sharing agreements. *Bonilla* dismissed a nonlawyer’s claim for payments tied to referred cases; *Ballan* likewise rejected a nonlawyer’s claim to a share of attorneys’ fees. [*Bonilla v. Rotter*, 36 A.D.3d 534, 535 (1st Dep’t 2007)](https://www.nycourts.gov/REPORTER/3dseries/2007/2007_00449.htm); [*Ballan v. Sirota*, 163 A.D.3d 516, 517 (2d Dep’t 2018)](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2018/2018_05014.htm).

The proposed payment also rewards the website for obtaining clients, contrary to Rule 7.2(a). The website could instead sell compliant advertising or neutral internet leads for a fee **unrelated to the law firm’s legal fees**, provided it does not recommend particular lawyers or imply that referrals are unpaid. [22 N.Y.C.R.R. § 1200.0, Rule 7.2(a) & cmt. 1](https://www.nycourts.gov/ad3/agc/rules/22NYCRR-Part-1200.pdf).

### Legal research memo

**Question.** What recording-consent law applies when a New York doctor uses an AI scribe during a visit, including a video visit with a patient in another state?

**Analysis.** New York generally permits a participant to record a conversation, or authorize a scribe to record it, with one party’s consent. [N.Y. Penal Law §§ 250.00, 250.05](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/PEN/250.00); [*People v. Lasher*, 58 N.Y.2d 962, 963 (1983)](https://law.counselstack.com/opinion/people-v-lasher-ny-1983). Federal law likewise permits interception with a party’s consent, but its permission does not displace a state’s more protective recording law. [18 U.S.C. § 2511(2)(d)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/2511); [*Kearney v. Salomon Smith Barney, Inc.*, 39 Cal. 4th 95, 103–04 (2006)](https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2006/s124739.html).

For an interstate video visit, **the doctor’s New York location alone does not settle the question**. Applying New York choice-of-law rules, *Locke* selected New York law for a claim by a person *in New York* whose call was recorded by someone in California, locating the alleged privacy injury where that person was. [*Locke v. Aston*, 31 A.D.3d 33, 37–38 (1st Dep’t 2006)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2006/2006_02839.htm). Conversely, *Kearney* applied California’s all-party-consent rule to a business recording calls outside California with people in California. [39 Cal. 4th at 103–04, 124–26](https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2006/s124739.html); [Cal. Penal Code § 632(a)](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=632.).

**Conclusion.** For each video visit, determine where the patient actually is and check that state’s recording law. If it requires every participant’s consent, obtain and document that consent **before** activating the scribe. The precise result depends on that state’s statute and the forum’s choice-of-law rules.

## Legal research memo

**Question.** What recording-consent law applies when a New York doctor uses an AI scribe during a video visit with a patient in another state?

**Answer.** For the visit’s audio, federal law permits recording with the prior consent of one participant, subject to its statutory exception for recordings made to further a criminal or tortious act. [18 U.S.C. § 2511(2)(d)](https://usc-cdn.house.gov/view.xhtml?edition=prelim&num=0&req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title18-section2511). New York likewise permits a participating doctor to consent to recording; its eavesdropping prohibition turns on recording without a participant’s consent. [N.Y. Penal Law §§ 250.00(1), (2), (6), 250.05](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/PEN/250.00); [*Locke v. Aston*, 31 A.D.3d 33, 35–36 (1st Dep’t 2006)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2006/2006_02839.htm).

**The patient’s location also matters.** New York’s one-party rule does not settle whether the patient’s state law applies. In *Locke*, a New York court applied New York law to a New York participant’s claim about a call recorded in California. Conversely, the California Supreme Court applied California’s all-party consent rule to calls recorded in Georgia with clients in California. [*Locke*, 31 A.D.3d at 37–38](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2006/2006_02839.htm); [*Kearney v. Salomon Smith Barney, Inc.*, 39 Cal. 4th 95, 124–31 (2006)](https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2006/s124739.html); [Cal. Penal Code § 632(a)](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=632.).

**Practical rule.** Determine where the patient is *during each visit* and check that state’s recording statute. For a repeatable interstate scribe workflow, disclose audio recording and obtain the patient’s consent before it begins, as well as the doctor’s. That satisfies the all-party rule illustrated by California; it also avoids treating the doctor’s New York location as a blanket exemption. The cited interstate cases concern telephone calls, so their application to a video platform is an inference from their reasoning and the statutes’ coverage of recorded communications.

**Draft legal research memo — New York and federal law as of September 28, 2026**

**Question presented.** May a New York youth basketball app publish box scores and highlight clips identifying 14-year-old players without parental releases?

**Short answer.** Likely yes for genuine game coverage, but the app needs a parent’s written consent before using a minor’s name or likeness in advertising or for trade. This distinction depends on how the clips and player pages appear in the app.

**Analysis.** New York Civil Rights Law §§50–51 govern use of a living person’s name or likeness for advertising or trade. For a minor, §50 calls for written consent from a parent or guardian. The New York Court of Appeals has recognized a public-interest exception where a minor’s image has a real relationship to the reported subject (*Messenger v. Gruner + Jahr*). Box scores and clips illustrating games likely fit that rule. Using the same player in an app ad, sales pitch, or promotion of a paid recruiting profile presents a different question under §§50–51.

The New York Child Data Protection Act may also govern **personal data of teen app users** if the app knows they are minors or is primarily directed to minors. It does not follow from the stated facts alone that every player shown is an app user. For covered users aged 13–17, processing must meet the Act’s necessity or consent rules, and sale of their personal data is barred (GBL §§899-ee, 899-ff).

Federal COPPA concerns services directed to children **under 13**, or operators with actual knowledge that they collect personal information from children under 13. Showing 14-year-olds alone does not trigger it (15 U.S.C. §6501 et seq.; 16 C.F.R. Part 312).

**Question presented.** Which recording-consent laws govern a New York doctor’s video visit with a patient in another state?

**Short answer.** New York generally permits a participant to consent to recording a conversation, including recording through a tool acting with that participant’s consent. The federal rule for covered interstate communications also permits one-party consent, absent a criminal or tortious purpose. Neither rule assures that a recording is lawful where the patient is located. (N.Y. Penal Law §§ 250.00, 250.05; 18 U.S.C. § 2511(2)(d).)

**Analysis.** The patient’s state may require every participant’s consent. California requires all-party consent for recording a confidential communication; Florida and Washington also impose all-party requirements for covered communications. (Cal. Penal Code § 632; Fla. Stat. § 934.03(2)(d); Wash. Rev. Code § 9.73.030.) In *Kearney v. Salomon Smith Barney, Inc.* (Cal. 2006), California’s highest court applied its recording law to calls with California clients recorded by a firm in Georgia. That decision controls California courts, not New York courts; the applicable law for another state and a particular video visit depends on that state’s statute and the forum’s choice-of-law analysis.

For visits crossing state lines, obtain and document the doctor’s and patient’s express consent **before** the scribe records or transcribes. Counsel should check the patient’s state and the scribe vendor’s role for each workflow.
